title: Secure Multi-Tenant AI Platform
subtitle: Serve 500 tenants on one shared AI platform while making a cross-tenant read, cache hit or model-context leak impossible rather than unlikely.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: Outcome, stakeholders and discovery
practice_prompts.hint: Which answers change residency, tiering or budgets?

practice_prompts.label: Tenant context and the seven layers
practice_prompts.hint: Where does the tenant come from, and what refuses an unscoped request at each layer?

practice_prompts.label: Quotas, fairness, regions and cost
practice_prompts.hint: Separate rate limits from fair queuing and justify the dedicated threshold.

practice_prompts.label: Failures, release gate and rollout
practice_prompts.hint: What fails closed, what degrades, and what evidence promotes a phase?

rubric: Derived tenant context from verified identity once and refused request-body or client-header tenant IDs.
Named all seven layers and showed the store refusing an unscoped read, including the RLS owner/superuser/BYPASSRLS caveat.
Checked quota and budget before inference and explained why a fair queue differs from a rate limit.
Justified the dedicated tier with the cost equation and measurable thresholds, not customer size.
Kept residency and retention covering logs, backups and derived indexes, and offboarding with a verified inventory.
Separated fail-closed security defects from capacity degradation and walked detect, refuse, contain, recover, prevent.
Diagnosed the Acme/Globex leak trace-first as an isolation failure with rollback, cache purge and a non-bypassable predicate.
Gated release on an adversarial suite with zero confirmed incidents and rolled out internal, shared, then dedicated with owners.
